correctedForm: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਆਪਣੇ ਪਰਿਵਾਰ ਨਾਲ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਅਤ ਮਹਿਸੂਸ ਹੁੰਦਾ ਹੈ। / ਮੈਨੂੰ ਆਪਣੇ ਪਰਿਵਾਰ ਨਾਲ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਅਤ ਮਹਿਸੂਸ ਹੁੰਦਾ ਹੈ।
meaningNote: The English translation matches the intended gloss.

nativeScript: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਗਰਮ ਚਾਹ ਚੰਗੀ ਲੱਗਦੀ ਹੈ।
romanized: mainu garam chaah changi lagdi hai.

nativeScript: ਅਸੀਂ ਰੋਟੀ ਨਾਲ ਸਬਜ਼ੀ ਖਾਂਦੇ ਹਾਂ।
romanized: asi roti naal sabzi khaande haan.

nativeScript: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਸਮਝ ਨਹੀਂ ਆਈ, ਕਿਰਪਾ ਕਰਕੇ ਫਿਰ ਦੱਸੋ।
english: I didn't understand; please say it again.
romanized: mainu samajh nahin aai, kirpa karke phir daso.
blindTranslation: I didn’t understand; please tell me again.
meaningNote: Both English versions express the same request to repeat something after not understanding it.
ਖਾਣਾ ਦਿਓ means “Give food / Give the food,” not specifically “Give me food.” The blind translation adds an unstated recipient.

nativeScript: ਸਾਨੂੰ ਭੋਜਨ ਨਾਲ ਥੋੜ੍ਹਾ ਮੱਖਣ ਚਾਹੀਦਾ ਹੈ।
english: We want a little butter with the meal.
romanized: saanu bhojan naal thora makhan chaahida hai.
blindTranslation: We need a little butter with the food.
meaningNote: “Need” and “want” differ slightly in English, but the Punjabi sentence means wanting/being in need of a little butter with the meal, so the gloss is close enough.

nativeScript: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਪਰਾਂਠਾ ਅਤੇ ਚਟਨੀ ਦਾ ਸੁਆਦ ਚੰਗਾ ਲੱਗਦਾ ਹੈ।
english: I like the taste of parantha and chutney.
romanized: mainu parantha ate chatni da swaad changa lagda hai.
blindTranslation: I like the taste of paratha and chutney.
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss; “paratha” vs “parantha” is only a spelling/romanization variant.

nativeScript: ਉਸ ਨੂੰ ਦਹੀਂ ਅਤੇ ਅੰਬ ਪਸੰਦ ਹਨ।
romanized: us nu dahi ate amb pasand han.
meaningNote: The Punjabi sentence says 'yogurt and mangoes' (plural/collective with ਅੰਬ), while the intended gloss is 'yogurt and mango' singular.

nativeScript: ਬੱਚਿਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਮਿੱਠੀ ਖੀਰ ਬਹੁਤ ਪਸੰਦ ਹੈ।
english: The children like sweet kheer very much.
romanized: bachian nu mithi kheer bahut pasand hai.
meaningNote: Same meaning; word order/intensity are natural variants.

nativeScript: ਮਾਫ਼ ਕਰਨਾ ਜੀ, ਮੈਂ ਥੋੜ੍ਹਾ ਦੇਰ ਹੋ ਗਿਆ।
english: Sorry, I am a little late.
romanized: maaf karna ji, main thoda der ho gaya.
meaningNote: The Punjabi sentence naturally means “Sorry, I’m a little late.”

english: Thank you, that is your kindness.
blindTranslation: Thank you, it is your kindness.
meaningNote: The blind translation and intended gloss are effectively equivalent; the slight difference between "it is" and "that is" does not change the meaning here.

nativeScript: ਸ਼ੁਭ ਰਾਤਰੀ, ਤੁਸੀਂ ਸਭ ਖੁਸ਼ ਰਹੋ।
romanized: shubh ratri, tusi sab khush raho.
blindTranslation: Good night, may you all remain happy.

meaningNote: नमः means “salutations” or “obeisance,” not a neutral “hello.” The Sanskrit sentence is grammatical, but the blind translation is not fully equivalent to the intended gloss.
The Sanskrit says 'excellent' (उत्तमः), while the intended gloss is 'good.' These are close but not equivalent.

blindTranslation: Please forgive me; I am late.

english: How are you, friend? I am fine.
blindTranslation: How are you, friend? I am well.
meaningNote: "I am well" and "I am fine" are equivalent here.

blindTranslation: Today I am staying at home.
meaningNote: Both render the present tense naturally; the difference between "am staying" and "stay" is not meaningful here.

blindTranslation: Now I am listening; you speak.

meaningNote: नमः means “salutation(s)” or “hail,” not specifically “hello.” The blind translation is close, but not fully equivalent to the intended gloss.

nativeScript: अहं तत्र गच्छामि, त्वं अत्र तिष्ठ।
english: I go there, you wait here.
romanized: aham tatra gacchami, tvam atra tishtha.
blindTranslation: I am going there; you stay here.
meaningNote: "stay here" and "wait here" are close in this imperative context; the Sanskrit is natural and conveys the intended sense.

nativeScript: श्वः अहं सर्वं पश्यामि, ततः वदामि।
english: Tomorrow I will see everything, then I will speak.
romanized: shvah aham sarvam pashyami, tatah vadami.
blindTranslation: Tomorrow I will see everything; then I will speak.

grammarIssue: The imperative should be in the 2nd person singular middle/passive-style form for 'sit down': उपविशस्व (or more commonly उपविश). Also कृपया is better understood as an indeclinable politeness adverb, but the main issue is that उपविश is not the correct imperative ending here.
meaningNote: "Please sit down now." matches the intended gloss.

blindTranslation: You speak again; I am listening.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means “You speak again; I am listening.” The intended gloss “Speak again, I am listening.” is more natural as an imperative, but the given translation matches the Sanskrit more closely.
As Sanskrit, मम पिता भोजनं करोति literally means 'my father makes/does food' rather than 'my father eats food.' For 'eats,' one would normally use खादति or a similar verb.
पठति can mean both 'reads' and more generally 'studies' in context.
"ਇੱਕ" corresponds to "one/a," so the blind translation "I need a ball" matches the intended gloss.

english: Today I come with a friend.
blindTranslation: Today I am coming with my friend.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit is grammatical and the English renderings are equivalent in meaning; the distinction between "am coming" and "come" is stylistic/aspectual rather than semantic here.

blindTranslation: My grandfather is resting at home.

nativeScript: मम मातुलः मम सह भोजनं करोति।
english: My maternal uncle eats with me.
romanized: mama mātulaḥ mama saha bhojanam karoti.
blindTranslation: My maternal uncle eats with me.
grammarIssue: The postposition सह should govern the instrumental, so मम सह is ungrammatical. The sentence also sounds less natural with भोजनं करोति for 'eats' in this context.
correctedForm: मम मातुलो मया सह भोजनं करोति।
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss.

blindTranslation: Thank you; may you give your help.
construction: optative with transitive verb ददातु plus object सहायतां
grammarIssue: ददातु is optative singular, but with the subject implied as 'you' in the polite request, the natural Sanskrit would use the 2nd person imperative/precative sense, and सहायतां is an awkward object with दा in this context. More idiomatic is an imperative/request form with सहायता or simply help in another construction.
meaningNote: The blind translation means 'may you give your help,' while the intended gloss is a polite request 'please give help.' The Sanskrit as written also does not naturally express the intended gloss.

blindTranslation: My maternal aunt comes to the house.

english: My grandson does not see grandfather.
blindTranslation: My grandson does not see his grandfather.
meaningNote: The blind translation adds the possessive 'his,' but the intended gloss is still naturally conveyed by the Sanskrit.

nativeScript: मम कुटुम्बे माता पिता च सन्ति।
english: In my family, my mother and father are there.
romanized: mama kutumbe mata pita ca santi.
blindTranslation: There are a mother and a father in my family.

nativeScript: मम स्वजनाः मम कुटुम्बे सुखेन वसन्ति।
english: My relatives live happily in my family.
romanized: mama svajanāḥ mama kutumbe sukhena vasanti.
blindTranslation: My relatives live happily in my family.
grammarIssue: The locative phrase is awkward/incorrect for the intended meaning. Mama kutumbe can mean 'in my family,' but with svajanāḥ it is more natural to say te/ete mama kutumbe vasanti, or use a more idiomatic possessive construction. Also, the sentence is stylistically repetitive with mama twice.
correctedForm: मम स्वजनाः सुखेन मम कुटुम्बे वसन्ति।
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss.
The Sanskrit sentence means 'I am alone' / 'I am by myself' (ekākī), which is not equivalent to 'I am lonely' as intended here.
प्रसन्नः can mean “pleased/happy”; the blind translation matches the intended gloss closely enough.

english: I am glad to get a friend.
blindTranslation: Having obtained my friend, I am delighted.

english: I am amazed by the new word.
blindTranslation: I am astonished by the new word.

nativeScript: अहं नूतनं कार्यं दृष्ट्वा विस्मितः अस्मि।
english: I am surprised after seeing the new task.
romanized: aham nutanam karyam drishtva vismitah asmi
blindTranslation: Seeing the new task, I am astonished.

meaningNote: प्रफुल्लः can mean cheerful/delighted; the blind translation matches the intended gloss closely enough.

english: I feel a little different inside.
blindTranslation: There is something different in my mind.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means more literally 'there is something different in my mind'; it does not naturally convey 'I feel a little different inside.' The English gloss is interpretive and shifts the subject/state.
काचम् means “glass”; the intended gloss is “cup” (usually कपम् or पानपात्रम् depending on context).

blindTranslation: I am happy in the lesson.
grammarIssue: सामान्यतः ‘पाठे’ (in a lesson/class) के साथ भाववाचक विशेषण ‘सुखी’ के बजाय ‘सुखेन/सुखी’ का प्रयोग यहाँ अस्वाभाविक है; यदि अर्थ ‘comfortable’ है तो ‘सुखेन अस्मि’ नहीं, बल्कि ‘सुखम् अनुभवामि’ या ‘पाठे सुखम् अस्ति’ जैसा रूप अधिक स्वाभाविक होगा. ‘सुखी अस्मि’ का अर्थ भी ‘I am happy’ होता है, न कि ‘comfortable’.
meaningNote: Blind translation says “I am happy in the lesson,” but intended gloss is “I am comfortable in class.” These are not equivalent, and the Sanskrit sentence also more naturally means “I am happy.”

english: For me, the curd is tasty.

nativeScript: मम दम्पती गृहे सह भोजनं कुरुतः।
english: My parents eat together at home.
romanized: mama dampatī gr̥he saha bhojanam kurutaḥ.
blindTranslation: My spouses eat together at home.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means “my spouses / the two of us spouses,” since दम्पती is dual and refers to a married pair, not specifically “parents.” If the intended gloss is “My parents eat together at home,” the sentence should use a word for parents, e.g. मातापितरौ.

english: I take food on the plate.
blindTranslation: I take food in a pot.
meaningNote: Blind translation says 'in a pot,' while intended gloss says 'on the plate.' Sanskrit स्थाल्याम् means 'in/on a pan or dish' depending context, but the English renderings are not equivalent.
भक्ष्यं “edible thing/food” and बालकाय “to the boy/child” match the intended sense closely enough.

english: Let the two parents take the serving plate.
blindTranslation: Let the two parents take the food plate.
meaningNote: भक्ष्यपत्रम् here can naturally mean a plate/dish for food, so “food plate” and “serving plate” are close enough in this context.

english: Please put the salt in the container.
blindTranslation: Please place the salt in the container.

english: How should I hold the spoon?
blindTranslation: How should he take the ladle?
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means “How should he take/hold the ladle?” The blind translation matches this more closely than the intended gloss, which shifts the person to “I” and spoon to ladle.
The Sanskrit means “I take the pot,” while the intended gloss is “I take the plate.” स्थाली means pot/cooking pot, not plate.

english: In our table area, he serves the meal.
blindTranslation: In our school, food is served.
grammarIssue: अस्माकं शाले is awkward: शाले should be locative singular 'in the hall/room', but with अस्माकं it would more naturally be अस्माकं शालायाम् or simply शाले. More importantly, भोजनं परिवेषयति is active 'he/she serves the food,' not passive 'food is served.' The sentence as written also does not clearly express 'our table area' unless शाला is intended as 'hall/room.'
meaningNote: The blind translation is passive ('food is served in our school'), but the intended gloss is active ('he serves the meal') and refers to 'our table area,' not 'our school.'

english: Warm drinking water is in the cup.
blindTranslation: The hot water is in the glass.
construction: locative case with the noun काच
grammarIssue: काचे is not a natural or correct locative for 'glass/cup' here; the intended meaning requires a proper locative form such as काचे/काचायाम् only if the noun were actually 'glass' in that sense, but the common Sanskrit word here is पानपात्रे or कुम्भे/चषके depending on the vessel. Also पानीयं is better than पानीयं only if intended as 'drinking water'; the sentence as given is awkward.
meaningNote: The blind translation says 'hot water in the glass,' but the intended gloss is 'warm drinking water in the cup.' The Sanskrit sentence uses 'hot' rather than 'warm' and 'water' rather than clearly 'drinking water in a cup.'

english: At mealtime, I take the bowl.
blindTranslation: At mealtime, I take the bracelet.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means “bracelet,” since कटकम् = bracelet/armlet; it does not mean “bowl” (which would be पात्रम् or similar).
उष्णं can mean “hot” or “warm,” so the blind translation matches the intended gloss closely enough.

english: My rice bowl is in front.
blindTranslation: My food vessel is in front.

english: Please take the spoon for me.
blindTranslation: Please take the ladle for me.

nativeScript: अस्माकं भोजनम् उष्णं च स्वादु च अस्ति।
english: Our meal is warm and tasty.
romanized: asmākaṃ bhojanam uṣṇaṃ ca svādu ca asti
blindTranslation: Our food is hot and tasty.
meaningNote: उष्णं can cover both “hot” and “warm”; स्वादु matches “tasty.”

english: Mother serves the food on the table.
blindTranslation: The mother serves the food on the table.
grammarIssue: शालः is nominative singular masculine, but the intended sense requires a locative meaning 'on the table'; additionally the phrase is unnatural as written. The subject 'माता' also takes the verb fine, but the location should be expressed in the locative.
meaningNote: The blind translation and intended gloss are effectively the same meaning.
‘Accept the food’ and ‘take the food’ are equivalent here.

blindTranslation: Please forgive me; I am speaking.

meaningNote: The Sanskrit is an imperative/polite request meaning “Please, listen.” The blind translation adds “may you,” which is not quite equivalent.

grammarIssue: उपविशतु is an intransitive imperative meaning “let him/her sit” or “sit”; with शालः as nominative it yields “Shala should sit,” not “sit at the table.” For the intended meaning, the object/place should be in the locative, and the postposition/lexeme should be different if “table” is meant.
meaningNote: The blind translation says “Please have Shala sit down,” while the intended gloss is “Please sit at the table.” These are not equivalent.

The Sanskrit means roughly “Greetings; everything becomes/is auspicious.” The blind translation has a benedictive nuance (“may everything be auspicious”), while the intended gloss is closer to a simple statement: “Hello, everything is good.”

construction: The predicate adjective with भवति and the vocative greeting
grammarIssue: शुभसन्ध्या is not the natural idiomatic evening greeting in Sanskrit, and भवान् कुशलः भवति is an awkward way to say 'you are well' in a greeting. Also, bhavati here makes it sound like a statement about being, not a direct greeting.
meaningNote: The blind translation 'Are you well?' differs from the intended gloss 'you are well.'

english: Good day, we will meet again tomorrow.
blindTranslation: Good day. We shall meet again tomorrow.
Very well, I will see you today.
meaningNote: अहं पश्यामि is present tense, ‘I see,’ not future tense ‘I will see.’ The sentence matches the intended gloss more closely than the blind translation.

english: Bless you, and have a good journey.
blindTranslation: May there be blessings, and may there be a safe journey.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit means roughly 'May there be blessings, and may there be a good journey.' The blind translation adds 'safe' and renders the first clause as plural 'blessings,' while the intended gloss is the idiomatic 'Bless you.'

english: Thank you, you are very welcome.
blindTranslation: Thank you; you are most welcome.
O revered lady, please, I am coming.
grammarIssue: श्रीमती is not a proper vocative form here; as a direct address it should be in the vocative, and the word order is unnatural. Also, आगच्छामि means 'I am coming' but placing अहम् after it is redundant though not ungrammatical.
meaningNote: The blind translation 'O revered lady' is stronger than 'Madam'; the Sanskrit as written addresses a 'fortunate/married woman' rather than clearly 'madam.'

english: Good night, we will meet again tomorrow.
blindTranslation: Good night; we will meet again tomorrow.

construction: object case with the verb पश्यामि
grammarIssue: भवान् is nominative; as the direct object of पश्यामि it should be accusative. Also अहं is best written in sandhi as अहम् before a vowel.
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss.

english: Have a good journey, and go happily.
blindTranslation: Auspicious journey; may you go safely.
meaningNote: The blind translation preserves the intended sense closely enough; 'safely' is a natural rendering of सुखेन here, though 'happily/easily' is also possible.

english: Excuse me, I am coming late.
blindTranslation: Please forgive me; I am arriving late.

english: How are you? I say that all is well.
romanized: katham asti? ahaṃ sarvaṃ kuśalaṃ vadāmi.
blindTranslation: How is it? I say that all is well.
meaningNote: कथमस्ति? literally means “How is it?” The intended gloss “How are you?” is a different but close English rendering; the Sanskrit itself is fine. The second sentence matches the gloss.

grammarIssue: अष्ट should be अष्टान् here, as the direct object of गणयामि requires the accusative plural when counting discrete items.
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss.

grammarIssue: The numeral should be in the accusative object position; नव is not the right form here for 'nine' as the thing counted.
meaningNote: The blind translation means 'I count as nine,' while the intended gloss means 'I count nine.'

english: There are four seats in our room.
blindTranslation: There are four seats in our classroom.
meaningNote: The Sanskrit sentence means “There are four seats in our room.” The blind translation says “classroom,” which is more specific and not equivalent.
नव means “nine,” so the blind translation matches the intended gloss; however the Sanskrit sentence itself is grammatical only if the numeral is intended.

nativeScript: معاف ڪجو، مان سمجهان نه ٿو.
romanized: maaf kajo, man samjhaan na tho.

nativeScript: ڪير هتي آهي، ماءُ يا پيءُ؟
english: Who is here, mother or father?
romanized: keir hati aahe, maa'u ya pee'u?
blindTranslation: Who is here, mother or father?
Peace be upon you, I am here.
meaningNote: "سلام عليڪم" is a natural greeting and functions as "Hi/Hello" in context; the blind translation is acceptable.
The Sindhi sentence means “My mother is beautiful,” not “My mother is dear.”

english: Thank you, put the bread there.
blindTranslation: Thank you, put the bread there.

english: My father is in the room.
blindTranslation: My father is in the room.

nativeScript: ڇا ٻار کي هاڻي کاڌو گهرجي؟
english: Does the child need food now?
romanized: chha baar khe haani khaado ghurjhe?
blindTranslation: Does the child need food now?

meaningNote: رانديڪو کڻي ٿو means “takes/carries” in a broad sense, but the intended gloss is specifically “carries the toy”; the blind translation “takes the toy” is also acceptable, so the English is not exactly equivalent to the intended gloss.

nativeScript: منهنجي چاچي گهر ۾ چانهه ٺاهي ٿي.
english: My aunt makes tea at home.
romanized: muhn-ji chaachi ghar me chaah tehayee thi.
blindTranslation: My aunt makes tea at home.

nativeScript: اسان جي ڏاڏي ٻار کي سڏي ٿي.
romanized: asaan ji daadhi baar khe sadi thi.
blindTranslation: Our grandmother is calling the child.
construction: Verb aspect/agreement with feminine singular subject
grammarIssue: The sentence uses the progressive form "سڏي ٿي" (‘is calling’), but the intended gloss is habitual/present simple. For a natural native sentence matching the gloss, use the non-progressive present form.
correctedForm: اسان جي ڏاڏي ٻار کي سڏي ٿيءَ.
meaningNote: The blind translation says progressive ‘is calling,’ while the intended gloss is habitual ‘calls.’

nativeScript: اسان جو ڏاڏو اسان سان ڳالهائي ٿو.
romanized: asaan jo daadho asaan saan galhaaei tho.
meaningNote: "اسان سان ڳالهائي ٿو" can mean "talks to us" or "talks with us" in context; the blind translation is acceptable.

english: She is a little sad today.
blindTranslation: She is a little sad today.

nativeScript: منهنجو ڪٽنب اڄ گهر ۾ گڏ آهي.
english: My family is together at home today.
romanized: muhn-jo katand aaj ghar me گڏ aah-e.
blindTranslation: My family is together at home today.

nativeScript: مون کي نئين ڳالهه تي حيرانگي ٿي.
english: I was amazed at the new thing.
romanized: mun khe nayeen gaalh te hairaangi thi.
blindTranslation: I was surprised by the new matter.
meaningNote: "حيرانگي ٿي" matches being surprised/amazed, and "نئين ڳالهه تي" is compatible with "at the new thing/matter."

english: Put the serving tray on the table.
blindTranslation: Put the plate on the table.
meaningNote: "ٿال" means a tray/plate, but the blind translation says "the plate" while the intended gloss is "the serving tray." The Sindhi sentence itself fits the intended gloss more naturally as "tray."

nativeScript: منهنجي ماسي پنهنجو پٽ سان وٺي آئي آهي.
english: My maternal aunt has brought her son with her.
romanized: muhn-ji maasi penhjo pat saan vati aayi aah-e.
blindTranslation: My aunt has brought her son with her.
construction: possessive/reflexive pronoun with a comitative phrase
grammarIssue: "پنهنجو پٽ سان" is ungrammatical here. The reflexive possessive should agree with the subject's possessed noun phrase, and the comitative needs proper marking; a native form would be "پنهنجو پٽ ساڻ" or more naturally "پنهنجي پٽ کي ساڻ وٺي آئي آهي" depending on the intended structure.
correctedForm: منهنجي ماسي پنهنجو پٽ ساڻ وٺي آئي آهي.
meaningNote: The blind translation matches the intended gloss; "her son" vs "her son with her" is the same meaning here.

english: Put the roti on the plate.
blindTranslation: Put the bread on the plate.

nativeScript: اڄ مون کي شاد لڳي ٿو.
romanized: aaj mun khe shaad lagi tho.
grammarIssue: The adjective should agree in gender with the subject’s intended meaning, and the word choice is semantically wrong here. "شاد" is not the natural adjective for 'glad' in this structure; native Sindhi would say "اڄ مون کي خوشي ٿي ٿي" or "اڄ مون کي خوشي محسوس ٿئي ٿي" / "اڄ مون کي خوشي لڳي ٿي" depending on intended nuance. As written, "شاد لڳي ٿو" is unnatural, and with "مون کي" the predicate should not be masculine singular "لڳي ٿو" if referring to the speaker’s feeling state in a natural way.
